content.title: About
content.content: Raw oats are whole oat grains (Avena sativa) harvested and sold without any heat treatment. They have a mild nutty flavor, a slightly sweet aroma, and a firm texture. Oats are commonly used after soaking, cooking, or baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats belong to the grass family and are one of the oldest cultivated grains.
Raw oat kernels are called "groats" and become oatmeal only after processing.
Oats contain beta‑glucans – soluble fibers that help lower cholesterol.
Historically, oats were used as animal feed and in traditional medicine.
Oats grow best in temperate climates with adequate moisture.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help regulate blood sugar levels and reduce cholesterol.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support muscle function, nerve health, and blood formation.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in oats protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin aid in energy metabolism.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to oats.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Raw oats contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Although oats are naturally gluten‑free, they are often processed on the same equipment as wheat, so people with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free oats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw oats are typically soaked in water or milk for several hours, then used in smoothies, kefir, overnight oats, or as a base for oat bars. They can also be ground into flour for baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw oats in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth.
